transcript.text: new washer jumpin all over the kitchen on spin like its gonna take off?? only had it 2 days

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. That sounds alarming, but on a machine that's only two days old it's very rarely a faulty part. By far the most common cause is the transit (shipping) bolts still being in. They lock the drum solid for delivery, so the suspension can't do its job and the whole machine bucks about on spin. After that, the usual culprits are the machine not standing level or a foot being loose, or an awkward load. Stop using it until you've checked this, as a washer walking about can pull on its hoses. 1. Look at the back panel. You're looking for three or four large bolts, usually with plastic spacers. If they're there, that's probably your problem. Undo them with a spanner, pull out the spacers too, and fit the plastic blanking caps that normally come in the bag with the manual. Keep the bolts in case you ever move house.
2. Check it's level and firm. Press down on each top corner in turn. It shouldn't rock. All four feet should touch a solid floor with their lock nuts tightened up. If it rocks, adjust the loose foot and lock it. A springy wooden floor can also make it walk.
3. Think about the load. If it was a single heavy item like a bath mat, duvet or jeans on their own, or just a couple of items, that can throw it off balance. A normal mixed load should spin fine. Once you've done those, run a spin-only programme with the drum empty. If the bolts are already out, the machine is level and it still jumps about even when empty, that's not right for a new machine. Contact the retailer or the manufacturer under warranty rather than fixing it yourself. So first: are those bolts still in the back, or were they removed when it was installed?
[Helpful to see: image "Check the transit bolts have been removed" — Transit bolts hold the drum still for delivery and must be removed before use — a machine that bangs, walks or vibrates (especially when new or recently moved) often still has them fitted. They unscrew from the back of the machine. Typical layout — your machine may differ.]
just looked at the back, theres 3 big bolts with plastic bits still in it and one hole with a plastic cap in. is that them?? i never took anything out

With them in, the drum is locked rigidly to the cabinet, so instead of the suspension soaking up the spin, the whole machine gets thrown around. The capped hole is common: on some machines the fourth position is already capped at the factory, or one bolt was taken out before delivery. Either way, it's the three still in that matter. 1. Keep it switched off and unplugged, and pull it out far enough to reach the back comfortably. Mind the hoses.
2. Undo each bolt with a spanner or socket, turning anticlockwise until it comes right out. They're long, so it takes a few turns.
3. Make sure the plastic spacer comes out too. Sometimes it stays in the hole and you need to wiggle or pull it out. If a spacer is left inside, the drum can still be partly locked.
4. Push the plastic blanking caps into the holes. These are usually in the bag with the manual. This keeps fingers and dust out.
5. Keep the bolts and spacers somewhere safe in case you ever move it. Then push it back. Press each top corner to check it doesn't rock, and tighten any loose foot's lock nut. Run a spin-only programme with the drum empty. It should now sit fairly still with just a normal hum and some light movement as it speeds up. Then try an ordinary mixed load. A couple of days' use with the bolts in usually does no lasting harm. But if it still bucks about, bangs or makes a knocking or grinding noise once they're out and it's level, don't keep using it. Contact the retailer or manufacturer under warranty, since it's brand new. Let me know how the empty spin goes.
ok ill unplug it n try. i found a spanner and some plastic caps in the bag that was in the drum, is that what i use?

Yes, that's exactly what they're for. Manufacturers usually pack a spanner sized to fit the transit bolts, plus the blanking caps for the holes, in the bag left in the drum. 1. With it unplugged, fit the spanner on each bolt head and turn anticlockwise until the bolt comes right out. If the spanner slips or the bolt is very tight, an ordinary socket or adjustable spanner of the same size will do.
2. Check the plastic spacer has come out with each bolt. If one stays in the hole, pull or wiggle it free, because a spacer left inside can still hold the drum.
3. Press a cap firmly into each of the three holes until it clicks or sits flush.
4. Keep the bolts, spacers and spanner together somewhere safe for any future move. Then push the machine back, check it doesn't rock on its feet, and run that empty spin-only programme. If it now sits fairly steady, the bolts were the cause and you're sorted. If it still jumps about with the bolts out and it's level, stop using it and contact the retailer or manufacturer, as it's under warranty. Let me know how it goes.
ok got the bolts out n put the caps in. ran a rinse n spin and its much quieter now, bit of vibration but it stays put. is that normal?

Yes, that's normal. Every washing machine vibrates a bit on spin, especially as it ramps up to top speed, and you'll often feel a short wobble as it passes through certain speeds. What matters is that it now stays put and is much quieter. That shows the drum is free to move on its suspension as it should. What would make it a fault is if it starts walking across the floor again with ordinary loads, or you hear heavy banging, knocking, or a grinding or rumbling that gets worse as it speeds up. If that happens on a machine this new, contact the retailer or manufacturer under warranty. A tip to keep it steady: avoid washing a single heavy item like a bath mat or duvet on its own, and add a few towels to balance it. It's also worth pressing on each top corner now and then to check it hasn't started to rock, and tightening the foot lock nuts if it has. Keep those bolts for any future move. Is there anything else you'd like a hand with?
